content: The selection of sanitation services and their associated criteria should encompass the entire service chain, tailored to the specific needs of each country. This determination should be guided by a policy dialogue that acknowledges the universal right to sanitation services that are accessible, safe, health-protective, affordable, and culturally acceptable (De Albuquerque, 2014). These attributes, along with any additional sanitation criteria, should primarily be evaluated based on public health considerations. However, they also have implications for environmental sustainability, public convenience, cost, affordability, and equitable access to sanitation services. The prioritization of these factors will vary depending on the specific circumstances of each country or local government jurisdiction. Sanitation services may involve various fees, such as sewerage connection fees, charges for public or shared toilet use, sewerage tariffs, fees for pit emptying by utilities or public institutions, and faecal sludge tipping fees. Risk assessment is a critical component of sanitation interventions, ensuring that public health is protected by managing risks associated with excreta management throughout the sanitation chain—from the toilet to final disposal or reuse. This process involves identifying and prioritizing the highest risks and implementing system improvements through a combination of technological upgrades, enhanced operational procedures, and behavior change. Regulatory and standard-setting efforts should focus on specific components of the sanitation chain but may also address entire systems or their parts, such as sanitation by-laws or planning regulations. Stakeholder collaboration is essential for identifying and addressing sanitation issues. This requires the formation of a stakeholder group led by members with the appropriate authority, organizational skills, and interpersonal abilities. Risk assessments should be based on actual conditions rather than assumptions or imported data. Frontline government staff, such as public health workers, students, and community leaders, can play a vital role in data collection if properly organized, incentivized, and supervised. Regulatory mechanisms must be tailored to the diverse steps in the sanitation service chain, which may include planning and building regulations, reuse standards, utility regulations, treatment standards, licensing, occupational health and safety regulations, technical standards, and consumer protection. These mechanisms should be aligned with relevant national technical standards and procedures. In cases where sanitation facilities are individually constructed, such as on-site systems, national technical standards or consumer protection legislation may apply. In rural areas or informal settings, national guidelines may be more appropriate. Treatment standards for liquid effluent and sludge discharges should be legally defined and enforced, with incremental standards introduced to promote gradual improvements. Standards should be specific to the intended use or disposal environment rather than universally applied. Public health or nuisance abatement legislation should address unintended effluents, such as leakages from septic tanks or latrine pits. The regulation of sanitation services can be complex, depending on the nature of the service provider. Public utilities should have specific regulatory arrangements, while private enterprises may be regulated through contracts or licensing agreements. Licensing arrangements should specify service standards, inspection regimes, and remedies for non-compliance. Simplifying licensing requirements can reduce complexity and encourage service providers to enter the market. Enforcement of sanitation standards and regulations should involve a mix of incentives, promotion, and sanctions. Regulatory systems are more effective when developed in partnership with those being regulated, leveraging their practical experience. Sanitation standards must be monitored and enforced, with sufficient capacity for inspection and prosecution. Regulatory actions should only be invoked when realistic alternatives are available. National guidelines and training should support enforcement efforts, and responsible managers should review and report on enforcement activities annually. Sanitation requires coordinated action across multiple sectors, necessitating the establishment of a multi-sectoral platform for dialogue and planning. This platform should be supported by a secretariat and led by a senior ministry or bureau with a governance role. Political leadership is crucial for driving progress on sanitation, supported by evidence-based strategies and resource allocation. Accountability frameworks are essential for maintaining safe sanitation services. These frameworks should link sanitation to government budget processes, with dedicated budget lines and funding windows established where necessary. Local governments play a pivotal role and should be provided with resources and technical assistance. Environmental health authorities, typically within ministries of health, play a key role in sanitation. Their functions include sector coordination, setting health-protective norms and standards, health surveillance, program delivery, and overseeing sanitation behavior change interventions. They are also responsible for monitoring and enforcing sanitation safety standards across various settings. In summary, effective sanitation service delivery requires comprehensive planning, risk management, regulatory mechanisms, stakeholder collaboration, and accountability frameworks.
